reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents a branded Coinbase One Card promotion with bitcoin rewards subject to asset-based rates, eligible transactions, terms, and approval requirements. The availability and issuer disclosures frame it as a qualified commercial offer rather than a credential request or payment scheme.

citations.quote: Coinbase One Card | Turn every purchase into bitcoin.
Earn up to 4% back in bitcoin on every purchase, plus all of the benefits included in a Coinbase One membership.
Up to 4% Bitcoin back with every purchase.
Bitcoin-back rates are based on cardholder’s assets on Coinbase.
Terms, conditions, and limitations apply.

opening.argument: The central promise is explicitly tied to a viewer action: use this card for purchases and receive Bitcoin in return. The offer is therefore not merely about cryptocurrency; it solicits participation in a card-and-account arrangement by presenting purchases as a way to acquire a digital asset. The promotional language emphasizes that the reward follows every purchase, while the rate depends on assets already held on Coinbase. That combination makes the acquisition pathway conditional on both spending and maintaining a Coinbase relationship, rather than a straightforward no-strings reward.

citations.quote: Up to 4% Bitcoin back with every purchase.
Bitcoin-back rates are based on cardholder’s assets on Coinbase.
Turn every purchase into bitcoin.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling this a branded card promotion does not resolve the underlying solicitation. The defense repeats the headline reward and qualifications, but those qualifications confirm that viewers must participate through purchases and a Coinbase asset relationship to obtain the advertised benefit. Issuer names and approval language establish commercial packaging, not that the acquisition promise is clear, proportionate, or non-deceptive.

citations.quote: Earn up to 4% back in bitcoin on every purchase
Bitcoin-back rates are based on cardholder’s assets on Coinbase.
Subject to eligibility and approval.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The argument treats an ordinary conditional card reward as if it were an unearned asset giveaway. The materials state that the reward is tied to purchases, is only “up to” a stated amount, depends on the cardholder’s Coinbase assets, and is subject to eligibility and approval. Those facts show a disclosed financial-product promotion, not a promise that anyone can freely obtain Bitcoin.

citations.quote: Terms, conditions, and limitations apply.
Not all transactions are eligible purchases.
Subject to eligibility and approval.

opening.argument: Several risk signals appear together: a conspicuous “up to 4%” Bitcoin return, language portraying Bitcoin as an asset of exceptional performance, and a pitch to convert ordinary spending into crypto. The benefit is not presented as a modest conventional rebate; it is framed as turning everything purchased into Bitcoin. The rate also depends on assets held on Coinbase, so the apparent reward is linked to a pre-existing crypto position. Terms and exclusions may exist, but their presence does not eliminate the risk that the headline framing overstates how broadly viewers can obtain the advertised return.

citations.quote: Like the best performing asset of the last decade.
Turn everything you buy into Bitcoin.
Earn up to 4% back in bitcoin on every purchase
Bitcoin-back rates are based on cardholder’s assets on Coinbase.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense treats disclaimers as if they neutralize the promotional framing. But “up to 4%” and the Bitcoin-performance comparison remain the attention-grabbing claims, while asset-based rates and ineligible transactions materially narrow the apparent universality of “every purchase.” The question is not whether conditions are mentioned, but whether the headline reward and crypto framing could lead viewers to overestimate what they will receive.

citations.quote: Like the best performing asset of the last decade.
Not all transactions are eligible purchases.
Bitcoin-back rates are based on cardholder’s assets on Coinbase.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The cited language is ordinary comparative advertising and a qualified reward description, not evidence that the return is guaranteed or effortless. The offer expressly says “up to,” discloses asset-based rates, excludes some transactions, and states that terms and limitations apply. Those qualifications directly address the alleged overstatement and leave no basis for converting crypto-themed promotion into a deceptive-return claim.

citations.quote: Terms, conditions, and limitations apply.
Not all transactions are eligible purchases.
Up to 4% Bitcoin back with every purchase.

opening.argument: Although the presentation can be read as an explanation of a new financial product, its operative role is to drive adoption. The title tells viewers to turn every purchase into Bitcoin, the narration contrasts the product favorably with ordinary points, and the closing frame says it is available now. The content does not neutrally analyze costs, drawbacks, or alternatives; it directs attention toward obtaining and using a branded card for crypto rewards. That is participation-oriented promotion dressed in explanatory language.

citations.quote: Coinbase One Card | Turn every purchase into bitcoin.
This card doesn't give you points
The Coinbase OneCard does something different.
Turn everything you buy into Bitcoin.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense relies on branding and disclosures, but those features are consistent with an advertisement. Naming issuers and mentioning terms can make a solicitation look formal without changing its purpose. The available-now framing, favorable comparison with points, and repeated instruction to transform purchases into Bitcoin show that the content is steering viewers toward a product, not providing balanced consumer analysis.

citations.quote: This card doesn't give you points
It gives you back something of actual value.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A product advertisement can be persuasive without being a scam. The material identifies the card, describes the reward as limited, states that Coinbase assets affect the rate, notes exclusions and approval, and identifies the companies involved. The favorable presentation and availability frame show promotion, but they do not show an invented product, a concealed payment route, or an unconditional promise of free Bitcoin.
